claim: Transcriptional quiescence is an evolutionarily conserved trait that distinguishes embryonic primordial germ cells (PGCs) from their somatic neighbors.
source: Transcriptional quiescence, an evolutionarily conserved trait, distinguishes the embryonic primordial germ cells (PGCs) from their somatic neighbors.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract, drawing on established scientific knowledge about PGC biology.

claim: PGCs from embryos maternally compromised for germ cell-less (gcl) misexpress somatic genes.
source: In Drosophila melanogaster, PGCs from embryos maternally compromised for germ cell-less (gcl) misexpress somatic genes, possibly resulting in PGC loss.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations presented in the manuscript and references to prior studies.

claim: Misexpression of somatic genes in gcl mutant PGCs possibly results in PGC loss.
source: In Drosophila melanogaster, PGCs from embryos maternally compromised for germ cell-less (gcl) misexpress somatic genes, possibly resulting in PGC loss.
evidence: This is presented as a speculative connection between gene misexpression and PGC loss.

claim: Gcl is required during proteolytic degradation of the Torso receptor.
source: Recent studies documented a requirement for Gcl during proteolytic degradation of the terminal patterning determinant, Torso receptor.
evidence: This claim references recent studies (Pae et al., 2017) documenting this requirement.

claim: Sex-lethal (Sxl) is a biologically relevant transcriptional target of Gcl.
source: Here we demonstrate that the somatic determinant of female fate, Sex-lethal (Sxl), is a biologically relevant transcriptional target of Gcl.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ectopic expression of a degradation-resistant form of Torso (torsoDeg) can activate Sxl transcription in PGCs.
source: Underscoring the significance of transcriptional silencing mediated by Gcl, ectopic expression of a degradation-resistant form of Torso (torsoDeg) can activate Sxl transcription in PGCs, whereas simultaneous loss of torso-like (tsl) reinstates the quiescent status of gcl PGCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing Sxl transcription in torsoDeg embryos.

claim: Simultaneous loss of torso-like (tsl) reinstates the quiescent status of gcl PGCs.
source: Underscoring the significance of transcriptional silencing mediated by Gcl, ectopic expression of a degradation-resistant form of Torso (torsoDeg) can activate Sxl transcription in PGCs, whereas simultaneous loss of torso-like (tsl) reinstates the quiescent status of gcl PGCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing restoration of transcriptional quiescence in gcl;tsl double mutants.

claim: Embryos derived from mothers expressing torsoDeg in the germline display aberrant spreading of pole plasm RNAs.
source: Intriguingly, like gcl mutants, embryos derived from mothers expressing torsoDeg in the germline display aberrant spreading of pole plasm RNAs, suggesting that mutual antagonism between Gcl and Torso ensures the controlled release of germ-plasm underlying the germline/soma distinction.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations of pole plasm RNA distribution in torsoDeg embryos.

claim: Mutual antagonism between Gcl and Torso ensures the controlled release of germ-plasm underlying the germline/soma distinction.
source: Intriguingly, like gcl mutants, embryos derived from mothers expressing torsoDeg in the germline display aberrant spreading of pole plasm RNAs, suggesting that mutual antagonism between Gcl and Torso ensures the controlled release of germ-plasm underlying the germline/soma distinction.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings regarding pole plasm distribution.

claim: A Drosophila embryo undergoes 14 consecutive nuclear divisions to give rise to the cellular blastoderm following fertilization.
source: Following fertilization, a Drosophila embryo undergoes 14 consecutive nuclear divisions to give rise to the cellular blastoderm.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila embryonic development, supported by citation (Farrell and O'Farrell, 2014).

claim: Initial nuclear divisions in Drosophila embryos take place in the center of the embryo.
source: While the initial nuclear divisions take place in the center of the embryo, the nuclei begin to migrate toward the periphery around nuclear cycle (NC) 4–6 and reach the cortex at NC9/10 (Farrell and O'Farrell, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila embryonic development, supported by citation.

claim: Nuclei begin to migrate toward the periphery around nuclear cycle 4-6 in Drosophila embryos.
source: While the initial nuclear divisions take place in the center of the embryo, the nuclei begin to migrate toward the periphery around nuclear cycle (NC) 4–6 and reach the cortex at NC9/10 (Farrell and O'Farrell, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila embryonic development, supported by citation.

claim: Nuclei reach the cortex at nuclear cycle 9/10 in Drosophila embryos.
source: While the initial nuclear divisions take place in the center of the embryo, the nuclei begin to migrate toward the periphery around nuclear cycle (NC) 4–6 and reach the cortex at NC9/10 (Farrell and O'Farrell, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila embryonic development, supported by citation.

claim: Before bulk nuclear migration commences, a few nuclei move toward the posterior of the embryo and enter the pole plasm.
source: Even before bulk nuclear migration commences, a few nuclei move toward the posterior of the embryo, enter a specialized, maternally derived cytoplasm known as the pole plasm, and induce the formation of pole buds (PBs) (Williamson and Lehmann, 1996; Wilson and Macdonald, 1993; Wylie, 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PGC formation, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Centrosomes associated with nuclei that enter the pole plasm trigger the release of pole plasm constituents from the posterior cortex.
source: The centrosomes associated with these nuclei trigger the release of pole plasm constituents from the posterior cortex and orchestrate precocious cellularization to form the primordial germ cells (PGCs), the progenitors of the germline stem cells in adult gonads (Lerit and Gavis, 2011; Raff and Glover, 1989).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PGC formation, supported by citations.

claim: Centrosomes orchestrate precocious cellularization to form primordial germ cells (PGCs).
source: The centrosomes associated with these nuclei trigger the release of pole plasm constituents from the posterior cortex and orchestrate precocious cellularization to form the primordial germ cells (PGCs), the progenitors of the germline stem cells in adult gonads (Lerit and Gavis, 2011; Raff and Glover, 1989).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PGC formation, supported by citations.

claim: PGCs are the progenitors of the germline stem cells in adult gonads.
source: The centrosomes associated with these nuclei trigger the release of pole plasm constituents from the posterior cortex and orchestrate precocious cellularization to form the primordial germ cells (PGCs), the progenitors of the germline stem cells in adult gonads (Lerit and Gavis, 2011; Raff and Glover, 1989).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PGC biology, supported by citations.

claim: Somatic nuclei continue synchronous divisions after they reach the surface of the embryo until nuclear cycle 14 when they cellularize.
source: Unlike pole cell nuclei, somatic nuclei continue synchronous divisions after they reach the surface of the embryo until NC 14 when they cellularize (Blythe and Wieschaus, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila embryonic development, supported by citation.

claim: Newly formed PGCs undergo only one or two asynchronous divisions before exiting the cell cycle.
source: Although newly formed PGCs divide after they are formed, they undergo only one or two asynchronous divisions before exiting the cell cycle.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PGC behavior.

claim: Transcription commences in the embryo during nuclear cycle 6-7 when a select number of genes are active.
source: Transcription commences in the embryo during NC 6–7 when a select number of genes are active (Ali-Murthy et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about zygotic genome activation, supported by citation.

claim: Transcription is more globally upregulated when nuclei reach the surface of the embryo.
source: Transcription is more globally upregulated when the nuclei reach the surface, and by the end of NC 14, zygotic genome activation (ZGA) is complete (Ali-Murthy et al., 2013; Harrison and Eisen, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about zygotic genome activation, supported by citations.

claim: Zygotic genome activation (ZGA) is complete by the end of nuclear cycle 14.
source: Transcription is more globally upregulated when the nuclei reach the surface, and by the end of NC 14, zygotic genome activation (ZGA) is complete (Ali-Murthy et al., 2013; Harrison and Eisen, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about zygotic genome activation, supported by citations.

claim: The transition to zygotic genome activation is marked by high levels of phosphorylation of Serine 5 and Serine 2 in the C-terminal domain of RNA polymerase II.
source: This transition is marked by high levels of phosphorylation of residues Serine 5 (Ser5) and Serine 2 (Ser2) in the C-terminal domain (CTD) of RNA polymerase II (Schaner et al., 2003; Seydoux and Dunn, 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge about transcriptional regulation, supported by citations.

claim: In newly formed PGCs, transcription is switched off.
source: By contrast, in newly formed PGCs, transcription is switched off, and PGC nuclei have only residual amounts of Ser5 and Ser2 CTD phosphorylation (Deshpande, 2004; Martinho et al., 2004; Seydoux and Dunn, 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PGC transcriptional quiescence, supported by citations.

claim: PGC nuclei have only residual amounts of Ser5 and Ser2 CTD phosphorylation.
source: By contrast, in newly formed PGCs, transcription is switched off, and PGC nuclei have only residual amounts of Ser5 and Ser2 CTD phosphorylation (Deshpande, 2004; Martinho et al., 2004; Seydoux and Dunn, 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PGC transcriptional quiescence, supported by citations.

claim: Changes in chromatin architecture that accompany ZGA are blocked in PGCs.
source: Moreover, and consistent with their transcriptionally quiescent status, other changes in chromatin architecture that accompany ZGA are also blocked in PGCs (Schaner et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PGC chromatin state, supported by citation.

claim: nanos (nos), polar granule component (pgc), and germ cell-less (gcl) are required for establishing transcriptional quiescence in newly formed PGCs.
source: Three different genes, nanos (nos), polar granule component (pgc), and germ cell-less (gcl), are known to be required for establishing transcriptional quiescence in newly formed PGCs (Deshpande et al., 2005; Deshpande, 2004; Deshpande et al., 1999; Hanyu-Nakamura et al., 2008; Kobayashi et al., 1996; Leatherman et al., 2002; Martinho et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: PGCs in embryos from nos/pgc/gcl mothers fail to inhibit transcription.
source: The PGCs in embryos derived from mothers carrying mutations in these genes fail to inhibit transcription, and this compromises germ cell specification and disrupts germ cell migration.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the phenotypes of these mutants.

claim: Failure to inhibit transcription in nos/pgc/gcl mutants compromises germ cell specification and disrupts germ cell migration.
source: The PGCs in embryos derived from mothers carrying mutations in these genes fail to inhibit transcription, and this compromises germ cell specification and disrupts germ cell migration.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the phenotypes of these mutants.

claim: nos, pgc, and gcl share only a few targets.
source: Interestingly, these three genes share only a few targets, suggesting overlapping yet distinct mechanisms of action.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that these genes have different sets of targets.

claim: Nos is a translation factor.
source: Nos is a translation factor and thus must block transcription indirectly.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Nos protein function.

claim: Nos must block transcription indirectly.
source: Nos is a translation factor and thus must block transcription indirectly.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the fact that Nos is a translation factor.

claim: Nos interacts with Pumilio (Pum) to bind recognition sequences in the 3'-untranslated regions of mRNAs and inhibit their translation.
source: Together with the RNA-binding protein Pumilio (Pum), Nos interacts with recognition sequences in the 3'-untranslated regions (3'UTRs) of mRNAs and inhibits their translation (Asaoka et al., 2019; Sonoda and Wharton, 1999; Wharton and Struhl, 1991).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Nos-Pum function, supported by citations.

claim: The key mRNA target(s) that Nos-Pum repress to block transcription is currently unknown.
source: Currently, the key mRNA target(s) that Nos-Pum repress to block transcription is unknown; however, in nos and pum mutants, PGC nuclei display high levels of Ser5 and Ser2 CTD phosphorylation and activate transcription of gap and pair-rule patterning genes and the sex determination gene Sex-lethal (Sxl) (Deshpande et al., 2005; Deshpande et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: In nos and pum mutants, PGC nuclei display high levels of Ser5 and Ser2 CTD phosphorylation.
source: Currently, the key mRNA target(s) that Nos-Pum repress to block transcription is unknown; however, in nos and pum mutants, PGC nuclei display high levels of Ser5 and Ser2 CTD phosphorylation and activate transcription of gap and pair-rule patterning genes and the sex determination gene Sex-lethal (Sxl) (Deshpande et al., 2005; Deshpande et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge about nos and pum mutant phenotypes, supported by citations.

claim: In nos and pum mutants, PGC nuclei activate transcription of gap and pair-rule patterning genes and Sex-lethal (Sxl).
source: Currently, the key mRNA target(s) that Nos-Pum repress to block transcription is unknown; however, in nos and pum mutants, PGC nuclei display high levels of Ser5 and Ser2 CTD phosphorylation and activate transcription of gap and pair-rule patterning genes and the sex determination gene Sex-lethal (Sxl) (Deshpande et al., 2005; Deshpande et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge about nos and pum mutant phenotypes, supported by citations.

claim: pgc encodes a nuclear protein that binds to the transcriptional elongation kinase p-TEFb.
source: pgc encodes a nuclear protein that binds to the transcriptional elongation kinase p-TEFb, blocking Ser5 CTD phosphorylation (Hanyu-Nakamura et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Pgc protein function, supported by citation.

claim: Pgc blocks Ser5 CTD phosphorylation by binding to p-TEFb.
source: pgc encodes a nuclear protein that binds to the transcriptional elongation kinase p-TEFb, blocking Ser5 CTD phosphorylation (Hanyu-Nakamura et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Pgc protein function, supported by citation.

claim: In pgc mutant pole cells, Ser5 phosphorylation is enhanced.
source: In pgc mutant pole cells, Ser5 phosphorylation is enhanced, as is transcription of several somatic genes, including genes involved in terminal patterning (Deshpande, 2004; Martinho et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge about pgc mutant phenotypes, supported by citations.

claim: In pgc mutant pole cells, transcription of several somatic genes, including genes involved in terminal patterning, is enhanced.
source: In pgc mutant pole cells, Ser5 phosphorylation is enhanced, as is transcription of several somatic genes, including genes involved in terminal patterning (Deshpande, 2004; Martinho et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge about pgc mutant phenotypes, supported by citations.

claim: The primary function of nos and pgc appears to be blocking ZGA in PGCs.
source: While the primary function of nos and pgc appears to be blocking ZGA in PGCs, gcl has an earlier function, which is to turn off transcription of genes activated in somatic nuclei prior to nuclear migration (Leatherman et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the known functions of nos and pgc, supported by citation.

claim: gcl has an earlier function than nos and pgc, which is to turn off transcription of genes activated in somatic nuclei prior to nuclear migration.
source: While the primary function of nos and pgc appears to be blocking ZGA in PGCs, gcl has an earlier function, which is to turn off transcription of genes activated in somatic nuclei prior to nuclear migration (Leatherman et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge about gcl function, supported by citation.

claim: Targets of gcl include two X-chromosome counting elements (XCEs), scute (sc/sis-b) and sisterless-a (sis-a).
source: Targets of gcl include two X-chromosome counting elements (XCEs), scute (sc/sis-b) and sisterless-a (sis-a), that function to turn on the sex determination gene, Sxl, in female soma (Cline and Meyer, 1996; Salz and Erickson, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about gcl targets, supported by citations.

claim: scute (sc/sis-b) and sisterless-a (sis-a) function to turn on the sex determination gene, Sxl, in female soma.
source: Targets of gcl include two X-chromosome counting elements (XCEs), scute (sc/sis-b) and sisterless-a (sis-a), that function to turn on the sex determination gene, Sxl, in female soma (Cline and Meyer, 1996; Salz and Erickson, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about XCE function, supported by citations.

claim: gcl embryos fail to shut off sis-a and sis-b transcription in pole buds.
source: gcl embryos not only fail to shut off sis-a and sis-b transcription in PBs, but also show disrupted PGC formation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about gcl mutant phenotypes.

claim: gcl embryos show disrupted PGC formation.
source: gcl embryos not only fail to shut off sis-a and sis-b transcription in PBs, but also show disrupted PGC formation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about gcl mutant phenotypes.

claim: In some gcl embryos, PGC formation fails completely.
source: In some gcl embryos, PGC formation fails completely, while in other embryos only a few PGCs are formed (Cinalli and Lehmann, 2013; Jongens et al., 1992; Lerit et al., 2017; Robertson et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge about gcl mutant phenotypes, supported by citations.

claim: In some gcl embryos, only a few PGCs are formed.
source: In some gcl embryos, PGC formation fails completely, while in other embryos only a few PGCs are formed (Cinalli and Lehmann, 2013; Jongens et al., 1992; Lerit et al., 2017; Robertson et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge about gcl mutant phenotypes, supported by citations.

claim: gcl differs from nos and pgc in that it has an effect on the process of PGC formation.
source: In this respect, gcl differs from nos and pgc, which have no effect on the process of PGC formation, but instead interfere with the specification of PGC identity.
evidence: This is a comparison of the phenotypes of different mutants, based on established knowledge.

claim: nos and pgc have no effect on the process of PGC formation, but instead interfere with the specification of PGC identity.
source: In this respect, gcl differs from nos and pgc, which have no effect on the process of PGC formation, but instead interfere with the specification of PGC identity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about nos and pgc mutant phenotypes.

claim: When pole buds first form during nuclear cycle 9 in wild-type embryos, levels of CTD phosphorylation in pole buds are only marginally less than in nuclei elsewhere in the embryo.
source: They found that when PBs first form during NC 9 in wild-type (WT) embryos, levels of CTD phosphorylation PB are only marginally less than in nuclei elsewhere in the embryo.
evidence: This is a finding from Leatherman et al., 2002, cited in the manuscript.

claim: By nuclear cycle 10, there is a dramatic reduction in CTD phosphorylation in wild-type pole buds even before they cellularize.
source: However, by NC 10, there was a dramatic reduction in CTD phosphorylation even before PBs cellularize.
evidence: This is a finding from Leatherman et al., 2002, cited in the manuscript.

claim: In gcl mutant embryos, about 90% of the nuclear cycle 10 pole bud nuclei have CTD phosphorylation levels approaching that of somatic nuclei.
source: By contrast, in gcl mutant embryos, about 90% of the NC 10 PB nuclei had CTD phosphorylation levels approaching that of somatic nuclei.
evidence: This is a finding from Leatherman et al., 2002, cited in the manuscript.

claim: The number of nuclear cycle 10 pole bud nuclei with high CTD phosphorylation shows an inverse correlation with the number of PGCs in blastoderm stage gcl embryos.
source: Moreover, this number showed an inverse correlation with the number of PGCs in blastoderm stage gcl embryos.
evidence: This is a finding from Leatherman et al., 2002, cited in the manuscript.

claim: Wild-type blastoderm embryos have >20 PGCs per embryo.
source: Whereas WT blastoderm embryos have >20 PGCs per embryo, gcl embryos had on average just three PGCs under their culturing conditions.
evidence: This is a finding from Leatherman et al., 2002, cited in the manuscript.

claim: gcl embryos have on average just three PGCs under the culturing conditions used by Leatherman et al., 2002.
source: Whereas WT blastoderm embryos have >20 PGCs per embryo, gcl embryos had on average just three PGCs under their culturing conditions.
evidence: This is a finding from Leatherman et al., 2002, cited in the manuscript.

claim: Expression of the mouse homologue of Gcl protein, mGcl-1, can rescue the gcl phenotype in Drosophila.
source: Interestingly, expression of the mouse homologue of Gcl protein, mGcl-1, can rescue the gcl phenotype in Drosophila (Leatherman et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a finding from Leatherman et al., 2000, cited in the manuscript.

claim: A protein complex between mGcl-1 and the inner nuclear membrane protein LAP2β is thought to sequester E2F:D1 to reduce transcriptional activity of E2F:D1.
source: Supporting the conserved nature of the involvement of Gcl during transcriptional suppression, a protein complex between mGcl-1 and the inner nuclear membrane protein LAP2β is thought to sequester E2F:D1 to reduce transcriptional activity of E2F:D1 (Nili et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a finding from Nili et al., 2001, cited in the manuscript.

claim: Leatherman et al. postulated a connection between failing to turn off ongoing transcription and defects in PGC formation in gcl mutants.
source: The connection Leatherman et al. postulated between failing to turn off ongoing transcription and defects in PGC formation in gcl mutants is controversial and unresolved.
evidence: This is a statement about a model proposed by Leatherman et al.

claim: The connection between failing to turn off ongoing transcription and defects in PGC formation in gcl mutants is controversial and unresolved.
source: The connection Leatherman et al. postulated between failing to turn off ongoing transcription and defects in PGC formation in gcl mutants is controversial and unresolved.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field.

claim: The Leatherman et al. model predicts that a non-specific inhibition of polymerase II should be sufficient to rescue PGC formation in gcl embryos.
source: This model predicts that a non-specific inhibition of polymerase II should be sufficient to rescue PGC formation in gcl embryos.
evidence: This is a logical prediction from the Leatherman et al. model.

claim: Cinalli and Lehmann, 2013 found that the PGC formation defects seen in gcl embryos were not rescued after injection of the RNA polymerase inhibitor, α-amanitin.
source: However, Cinalli and Lehmann, 2013 found that the PGC formation defects seen in gcl embryos were not rescued after injection of the RNA polymerase inhibitor, α-amanitin.
evidence: This is a finding from Cinalli and Lehmann, 2013, cited in the manuscript.

claim: α-amanitin treatment disrupted somatic cellularization without impacting PGC formation in wild-type embryos.
source: Since α-amanitin treatment disrupted somatic cellularization without impacting PGC formation in WT embryos, they concluded that it effectively blocked polymerase transcription.
evidence: This is a finding from Cinalli and Lehmann, 2013, cited in the manuscript.

claim: Cinalli and Lehmann, 2013 concluded that α-amanitin effectively blocked polymerase transcription.
source: Since α-amanitin treatment disrupted somatic cellularization without impacting PGC formation in WT embryos, they concluded that it effectively blocked polymerase transcription.
evidence: This is a conclusion from Cinalli and Lehmann, 2013, cited in the manuscript.

claim: Pae et al., 2017 raised the possibility that inhibiting transcription in pole cell nuclei is a critical step in PGC formation.
source: On the other hand, subsequent experiments by Pae et al., 2017 raised the possibility that inhibiting transcription in pole cell nuclei is a critical step in PGC formation.
evidence: This is a statement about a possibility raised by Pae et al., 2017.

claim: Gcl is a substrate-specific adaptor for a Cullin3-RING ubiquitin ligase that targets the terminal pathway receptor tyrosine kinase, Torso, for degradation.
source: These authors showed that Gcl is a substrate-specific adaptor for a Cullin3-RING ubiquitin ligase that targets the terminal pathway receptor tyrosine kinase, Torso, for degradation.
evidence: This is a finding from Pae et al., 2017, cited in the manuscript.

claim: The degradation of Torso would be expected to prevent activation of the terminal signaling cascade in PGCs.
source: The degradation of Torso would be expected to prevent activation of the terminal signaling cascade in PGCs.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the finding that Gcl targets Torso for degradation.

claim: In the soma, Torso-dependent signaling activates the transcription of several patterning genes, including tailless.
source: In the soma, Torso-dependent signaling activates the transcription of several patterning genes, including tailless, that are important for forming terminal structures at the anterior and posterior of the embryo (Casanova and Struhl, 1989; Klingler et al., 1988; Martinho et al., 2004; Pignoni et al., 1992; Strecker et al., 1989).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Torso signaling, supported by citations.

claim: Patterning genes activated by Torso-dependent signaling are important for forming terminal structures at the anterior and posterior of the embryo.
source: In the soma, Torso-dependent signaling activates the transcription of several patterning genes, including tailless, that are important for forming terminal structures at the anterior and posterior of the embryo (Casanova and Struhl, 1989; Klingler et al., 1988; Martinho et al., 2004; Pignoni et al., 1992; Strecker et al., 1989).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Torso signaling, supported by citations.

claim: By targeting Torso for degradation, Gcl would prevent the transcriptional activation of terminal pathway genes by the MAPK/ERK kinase cascade in PGCs.
source: Thus, by targeting Torso for degradation, Gcl would prevent the transcriptional activation of terminal pathway genes by the MAPK/ERK kinase cascade in PGCs.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the finding that Gcl targets Torso for degradation.

claim: Simultaneous removal of gcl and either torso-like (tsl) or torso resulted in rescue of germ cell loss induced by gcl.
source: Consistent with this possibility, simultaneous removal of gcl and either the Torso ligand modifier, torso-like (tsl) or torso resulted in rescue of germ cell loss induced by gcl.
evidence: This is a finding from Pae et al., 2017, cited in the manuscript.

claim: Pae et al., 2017 were unable to observe a similar rescue of gcl phenotype when they used RNAi knockdown to compromise components of the MAP kinase cascade known to act downstream of the Torso receptor.
source: Surprisingly, however, Pae et al., 2017 were unable to observe a similar rescue of gcl phenotype when they used RNAi knockdown to compromise components of the MAP kinase cascade known to act downstream of the Torso receptor (Ambrosio et al., 1989; Duffy and Perrimon, 1994; Furriols and Casanova, 2003).
evidence: This is a finding from Pae et al., 2017, cited in the manuscript.

claim: Pae et al., 2017 proposed that activated Torso must inhibit PGC formation via a distinct non-canonical mechanism that is both independent of the standard signal transduction pathway and does not involve transcriptional activation.
source: Based on these findings, they proposed that activated Torso must inhibit PGC formation via a distinct non-canonical mechanism that is both independent of the standard signal transduction pathway and does not involve transcriptional activation.
evidence: This is a proposal from Pae et al., 2017, cited in the manuscript.

claim: Leatherman et al., 2002 indicated that two of the key X chromosomal counting elements, sis-a and sis-b, were inappropriately expressed in gcl pole buds and PGCs.
source: The studies of Leatherman et al., 2002 indicated that two of the key X chromosomal counting elements, sis-a and sis-b, were inappropriately expressed in gcl PBs and PGCs.
evidence: This is a finding from Leatherman et al., 2002, cited in the manuscript.

claim: Transcription factors encoded by sis-a and sis-b function to activate the Sxl establishment promoter, Sxl-Pe, in somatic nuclei of female embryos.
source: Since transcription factors encoded by these two genes function to activate the Sxl establishment promoter, Sxl-Pe, in somatic nuclei of female embryos, their findings raised the possibility that Sxl might be ectopically expressed in PBs/PGCs of gcl embryos.
evidence: This is established knowledge about XCE function.

claim: In gcl embryos, Sxl transcription is inappropriately activated in pole buds and newly formed PGCs.
source: Here we show that in gcl embryos, Sxl transcription is indeed inappropriately activated in PBs and newly formed PGCs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Ectopic expression of Sxl in early embryos disrupts PGC formation similar to gcl.
source: Moreover, ectopic expression of Sxl in early embryos disrupts PGC formation similar to gcl.
evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: PGC formation defects in gcl embryos can be suppressed by knocking down Sxl expression using RNAi.
source: Supporting the conclusion that Sxl is a biologically relevant transcriptional target of Gcl, PGC formation defects in gcl embryos can be suppressed either by knocking down Sxl expression using RNAi or by loss-of-function mutations.
evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: PGC formation defects in gcl embryos can be suppressed by loss-of-function mutations in Sxl.
source: Supporting the conclusion that Sxl is a biologically relevant transcriptional target of Gcl, PGC formation defects in gcl embryos can be suppressed either by knocking down Sxl expression using RNAi or by loss-of-function mutations.
evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Loss of torso-like (tsl) in gcl embryos suppresses PGC formation defects.
source: As reported by Pae et al., 2017, we found that loss of torso-like (tsl) in gcl embryos suppresses PGC formation defects.
evidence: This is a finding of the study, confirming a result from Pae et al., 2017.

claim: Rescue of PGC formation defects in gcl;tsl embryos is accompanied by the reestablishment of transcriptional silencing in gcl PGCs.
source: However, consistent with a mechanism that is tied to transcriptional misregulation, rescue is accompanied by the reestablishment of transcriptional silencing in gcl PGCs.
evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Expression of a mutant form of Torso that is resistant to Gcl-dependent degradation (torsoDeg) ectopically activates transcription of sis-b in pole bud and PGC nuclei.
source: Lending further credence to the idea that transcription misregulation plays an important role in disrupting PGC development in gcl embryos, we found that expression of a mutant form of Torso that is resistant to Gcl-dependent degradation (hereafter referred to as torsoDeg Pae et al., 2017) ectopically activates transcription of two Gcl targets, sis-b and Sxl, in PB and PGC nuclei.
evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Expression of torsoDeg ectopically activates transcription of Sxl in pole bud and PGC nuclei.
source: Lending further credence to the idea that transcription misregulation plays an important role in disrupting PGC development in gcl embryos, we found that expression of a mutant form of Torso that is resistant to Gcl-dependent degradation (hereafter referred to as torsoDeg Pae et al., 2017) ectopically activates transcription of two Gcl targets, sis-b and Sxl, in PB and PGC nuclei.
evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Stabilization of Torso in early PGCs mimics the gcl phenotype of failure to properly sequester key PGC determinants in pole buds and newly formed PGCs.
source: In addition, stabilization of Torso in early PGCs also mimics another gcl phenotype, the failure to properly sequester key PGC determinants in PBs and newly formed PGCs.
evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Nuclear sis-b transcripts are not detected in wild-type pole buds or PGCs.
source: As shown in Figure 1a, nuclear sis-b transcripts are not detected in WT PBs or PGCs (n = 16 embryos).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: In 67% of gcl embryos, sis-b transcripts are observed in pole bud and PGC nuclei.
source: In contrast, in 67% of gcl embryos, we observed sis-b transcripts in PB and PGC nuclei (Figure 1b, n = 21 embryos, p=2.1e-05).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: sis-b transcripts are present most frequently in gcl pole buds.
source: sis-b transcripts are present most frequently in gcl PBs; however, we can also detect transcripts after PGC cellularization.
evidence: This is an observation from the smFISH experiments.

claim: sis-b transcripts can be detected after PGC cellularization in gcl embryos.
source: sis-b transcripts are present most frequently in gcl PBs; however, we can also detect transcripts after PGC cellularization.
evidence: This is an observation from the smFISH experiments.

claim: Leatherman et al. reported that sis-a is not properly turned off in gcl pole buds and PGCs.
source: Leatherman et al. reported that a second XCE, sis-a, is not properly turned off in gcl PBs and PGCs.
evidence: This is a finding from Leatherman et al., cited in the manuscript.

claim: runt is expressed in a subset of gcl pole bud nuclei and PGCs.
source: We found that like sis-b, runt is also expressed in a subset of gcl PB nuclei and PGCs (29% of gcl embryos, n = 11, p=0.009653), while it is never observed in WT PBs or PGCs.
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data.

claim: runt is never observed in wild-type pole buds or PGCs.
source: We found that like sis-b, runt is also expressed in a subset of gcl PB nuclei and PGCs (29% of gcl embryos, n = 11, p=0.009653), while it is never observed in WT PBs or PGCs.
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data.

claim: In experiments examining sis-b and runt transcription simultaneously, some pole bud/PGC nuclei expressed both XCEs, and some expressed only one or the other.
source: Curiously, in experiments where we examined sis-b and runt transcription simultaneously, we observed some PB/PGC nuclei that expressed both XCEs, and some that only expressed one or the other.
evidence: This is an observation from the smFISH experiments.

claim: Transcription during early embryogenesis is stochastic, as only a subset of nuclei express the same gene at any given time.
source: In this regard, it is important to keep in mind that transcription during early embryogenesis is stochastic, as only a subset of nuclei express the same gene at any given time (Fukaya et al., 2016; Muerdter and Stark, 2016; Zoller et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about transcriptional dynamics, supported by citations.

claim: Gcl is required to repress the transcription of XCEs in pole buds and PGCs.
source: Nonetheless, as WT PBs or PGCs never display sis-b transcripts, our data show that Gcl is required to repress the transcription of XCEs in PBs and PGCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The pattern of Sxl-Pe activity in the soma of gcl embryos is the same as wild-type.
source: In the soma, we found that the pattern of Sxl-Pe activity was indistinguishable between WT and gcl embryos, as Sxl-Pe transcripts are not detected prior to nuclear migration, nor are they observed in NC 10 somatic nuclei.
evidence: This is an observation from the smFISH experiments.

claim: Sxl-Pe transcripts are not detected prior to nuclear migration in wild-type and gcl embryos.
source: In the soma, we found that the pattern of Sxl-Pe activity was indistinguishable between WT and gcl embryos, as Sxl-Pe transcripts are not detected prior to nuclear migration, nor are they observed in NC 10 somatic nuclei.
evidence: This is an observation from the smFISH experiments.

claim: Sxl-Pe transcripts are not observed in nuclear cycle 10 somatic nuclei in wild-type and gcl embryos.
source: In the soma, we found that the pattern of Sxl-Pe activity was indistinguishable between WT and gcl embryos, as Sxl-Pe transcripts are not detected prior to nuclear migration, nor are they observed in NC 10 somatic nuclei.
evidence: This is an observation from the smFISH experiments.

claim: In approximately half of the embryos, Sxl-Pe transcripts are observed in somatic nuclei from nuclear cycle 11 until nuclear cycle 14.
source: In approximately half of the embryos, Sxl-Pe transcripts are observed in somatic nuclei from NC 11 until NC 14.
evidence: This is an observation from the smFISH experiments.

claim: In embryos with Sxl-Pe transcripts in somatic nuclei, two nuclear dots of hybridization are detected in most nuclei, indicating that they are female.
source: Moreover, in these embryos, two nuclear dots of hybridization are detected in most nuclei, indicating that they are female (Erickson and Quintero, 2007; Keyes et al., 1992).
evidence: This is an observation from the smFISH experiments, with interpretation based on established knowledge.

claim: In the remaining gcl and wild-type nuclear cycle 11-14 embryos, Sxl-Pe transcripts are not observed in somatic nuclei, indicating that these embryos are male.
source: In the remaining gcl and WT NC 11–14 embryos, Sxl-Pe transcripts are not observed in somatic nuclei, indicating that these embryos are male.
evidence: This is an observation from the smFISH experiments, with interpretation based on established knowledge.

claim: Sxl-Pe transcripts can be detected in pole buds and PGCs in 42% of gcl embryos.
source: As shown in Figure 1d, Sxl-Pe transcripts can be detected in PBs and PGCs in 42% of gcl embryos (n = 31 embryos, p=0.001593), while transcripts are not observed in WT PBs or PGCs (Figure 1c, n = 18 embryos).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Sxl-Pe transcripts are not observed in wild-type pole buds or PGCs.
source: As shown in Figure 1d, Sxl-Pe transcripts can be detected in PBs and PGCs in 42% of gcl embryos (n = 31 embryos, p=0.001593), while transcripts are not observed in WT PBs or PGCs (Figure 1c, n = 18 embryos).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The Sxl-Pe promoter remains active after pole buds cellularize in gcl embryos.
source: It is notable that the Sxl-Pe promoter remains active after the PBs cellularize, and nascent Sxl-Pe transcripts can be detected in PGC nuclei of gcl embryos, while they are never observed in the WT PGCs.
evidence: This is an observation from the smFISH experiments.

claim: Nascent Sxl-Pe transcripts can be detected in PGC nuclei of gcl embryos.
source: It is notable that the Sxl-Pe promoter remains active after the PBs cellularize, and nascent Sxl-Pe transcripts can be detected in PGC nuclei of gcl embryos, while they are never observed in the WT PGCs.
evidence: This is an observation from the smFISH experiments.

claim: Nascent Sxl-Pe transcripts are never observed in wild-type PGCs.
source: It is notable that the Sxl-Pe promoter remains active after the PBs cellularize, and nascent Sxl-Pe transcripts can be detected in PGC nuclei of gcl embryos, while they are never observed in the WT PGCs.
evidence: This is an observation from the smFISH experiments.

claim: In gcl embryos, Sxl-Pe transcripts are found in both female and male PGCs.
source: In gcl embryos, Sxl-Pe transcripts are found not only in female PGCs, as evidenced by Sxl-Pe expression in somatic nuclei, but also in male gcl PGCs, which lack somatic Sxl-Pe.
evidence: This is an observation from the smFISH experiments.

claim: The frequency of female gcl embryos expressing Sxl-Pe transcripts in their PGCs is somewhat higher than that of male gcl embryos.
source: In the NC 11–14 embryos examined, the frequency of female gcl embryos expressing Sxl-Pe transcripts in their PGCs is somewhat higher than that of male gcl embryos (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: Sxl-Pe promoter activity is turned on by XCEs (Sis-A, Sis-B, Runt) in a dose-dependent manner.
source: First, Sxl-Pe promoter activity is turned on by XCEs (Sis-A, Sis-B, Runt) in a dose-dependent manner, and these XCEs are also gcl targets.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Sxl-Pe regulation.

claim: There are two copies of the Sxl gene in females.
source: Second, there are two copies of the Sxl gene in females, which could increase the probability that it will be active in gcl mutants.
evidence: This is established knowledge about sex chromosome composition.

claim: Sxl protein can be detected in the PGCs of gcl embryos.
source: Sxl protein can be detected in the PGCs of gcl embryos (Figure 2A–D; WT control: n = 40; 2/40 Sxl positive PGC nuclei as opposed to gcl: n = 36; 16/36 Sxl positive, p=7.621e-05).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: The Sxl-Pe promoter is normally repressed by Gcl in pole buds and newly formed PGCs.
source: These data indicate that the Sxl-Pe promoter is normally repressed by Gcl in PBs and newly formed PGCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The failure to turn off the ongoing transcription of sis-b, sis-a (and possibly runt) likely contributes to the activation of Sxl-Pe in gcl pole buds and PGCs.
source: While the failure to turn off the ongoing transcription of sis-b, sis-a (and possibly runt) likely contributes to the activation of Sxl-Pe in gcl PBs and PGCs, the fact that activation of the promoter is earlier than normal and is subsequently observed in both female and male PGCs suggests that XCE activity may not be the only contributing factor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: The activation of Sxl-Pe in gcl pole buds and PGCs is earlier than normal.
source: While the failure to turn off the ongoing transcription of sis-b, sis-a (and possibly runt) likely contributes to the activation of Sxl-Pe in gcl PBs and PGCs, the fact that activation of the promoter is earlier than normal and is subsequently observed in both female and male PGCs suggests that XCE activity may not be the only contributing factor.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: XCE activity may not be the only contributing factor to Sxl-Pe activation in gcl pole buds and PGCs.
source: While the failure to turn off the ongoing transcription of sis-b, sis-a (and possibly runt) likely contributes to the activation of Sxl-Pe in gcl PBs and PGCs, the fact that activation of the promoter is earlier than normal and is subsequently observed in both female and male PGCs suggests that XCE activity may not be the only contributing factor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: Sxl protein is absent in the pole cells from wild-type embryos.
source: Sxl protein is absent in the pole cells from the control (wild-type [WT]) embryo (A) whereas some of the gcl mutant pole cells show presence of Sxl (B).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Some gcl mutant pole cells show presence of Sxl protein.
source: Sxl protein is absent in the pole cells from the control (wild-type [WT]) embryo (A) whereas some of the gcl mutant pole cells show presence of Sxl (B).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Only gcl mutant pole cells show Sxl protein in syncytial blastoderm stage female embryos.
source: Panels C and D: Syncytial blastoderm stage female embryos from mothers of the indicated genotype were stained using anti-Sxl antibody. Similar to pole buds, only gcl mutant pole cells show Sxl protein (D) as opposed to the control (C).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Sxl-specific signal is strong and uniform in the control embryo.
source: While Sxl-specific signal is strong and uniform in the control embryo, selective reduction in Sxl in the anterior is readily seen in the gcl-bcd 3'UTR embryo (marked with an asterisk).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Selective reduction in Sxl in the anterior is readily seen in the gcl-bcd 3'UTR embryo.
source: While Sxl-specific signal is strong and uniform in the control embryo, selective reduction in Sxl in the anterior is readily seen in the gcl-bcd 3'UTR embryo (marked with an asterisk).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Gcl alone is sufficient to repress Sxl.
source: This localized disruption of Sxl expression is coincident with the anterior expression of Gcl protein in the gcl-bcd-3'UTR embryos, indicating that Gcl alone is sufficient to repress Sxl.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gcl-bcd-3'UTR experiment.

claim: The number of PGCs in late syncytial and early cellular blastoderm mat-GAL4/UAS-Sxl embryos is reduced nearly twofold compared to mat-GAL4 embryos.
source: We compared the total number of PGCs in late syncytial and early cellular blastoderm (stage 4/5) mat-GAL4/UAS-Sxl with mat-GAL4 embryos. In WT, there are typically about 25 PGCs in stage 4/5 embryos. This number is reduced nearly twofold in mat-GAL4/UAS-Sxl embryos (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by PGC counting data shown in Figure 3.

claim: There are typically about 25 PGCs in stage 4/5 wild-type embryos.
source: We compared the total number of PGCs in late syncytial and early cellular blastoderm (stage 4/5) mat-GAL4/UAS-Sxl with mat-GAL4 embryos. In WT, there are typically about 25 PGCs in stage 4/5 embryos.
evidence: This is an observation from the PGC counting experiments.

claim: A reduction of PGCs was observed when nosGAL4-VP16 was used to drive UAS-Sxl expression in the germline.
source: A reduction of PGCs was also observed when we mated virgins carrying the germ cell-specific nosGAL4-VP16 promoter to UAS-Sxl males to drive expression in the germline (6.5 PGCs per gonad in nosGAL4/UAS-Sxl embryos, n = 15, compared to 10 PGCs per gonad in nosGAL4/+ control, n = 12 embryos).
evidence: This is supported by PGC counting data.

claim: Overexpression of Sxl in the germline impaired PGC migration.
source: Further, overexpression of Sxl in the germline impaired PGC migration. Figure 4 shows PGC migration defects in nosGAL4-VP16/UAS-Sxl embryos (3/21 UAS Sxl/+ control embryos showed >5 mispositioned PGCs as opposed to 9/17 nosGAL4-VP16/UAS-Sxl embryos; p=0.04).
evidence: This is supported by PGC migration data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Precocious expression of Sxl protein has deleterious effects on PGC development and behavior during early embryogenesis.
source: Taken together, these findings demonstrate that precocious expression of Sxl protein has deleterious effects on PGC development and behavior during early embryogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on Sxl overexpression.

claim: gcl;tsl embryos display a significant increase in the number of PGCs as compared to gcl embryos.
source: Figure 8 and Table 3 show that gcl;tsl embryos display a significant increase in the number of PGCs as compared to gcl embryos, and that the rescue is highly penetrant (p<2e-16, Figure 8D).
evidence: This is supported by PGC counting data shown in Figure 8 and Table 3.

claim: The rescue of PGC numbers in gcl;tsl embryos is highly penetrant.
source: Figure 8 and Table 3 show that gcl;tsl embryos display a significant increase in the number of PGCs as compared to gcl embryos, and that the rescue is highly penetrant (p<2e-16, Figure 8D).
evidence: This is supported by PGC counting data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Removal of tsl restores transcriptional quiescence in the pole buds/PGCs of gcl;tsl embryos.
source: Table 3 shows that removal of tsl restores transcriptional quiescence in the PBs/PGCs of gcl;tsl embryos (Figure 8 and Table 3, p=1e-06 and 1 for WT compared to gcl and gcl;tsl, respectively, by Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 8 and Table 3.

claim: Inactivation of the terminal signaling pathway by Gcl is critical for silencing transcription in pole buds and PGCs.
source: Taken together, these data confirm that inactivation of the terminal signaling pathway by Gcl is critical for silencing transcription in PBs and PGCs and that this silencing function plays an important role in PGC formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gcl;tsl rescue experiments.

claim: Transcriptional silencing plays an important role in PGC formation.
source: Taken together, these data confirm that inactivation of the terminal signaling pathway by Gcl is critical for silencing transcription in PBs and PGCs and that this silencing function plays an important role in PGC formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Both sis-b and Sxl-Pe transcripts are inappropriately expressed in the pole buds and PGCs of torsoDeg embryos.
source: Figure 9 shows that both sis-b and Sxl-Pe transcripts are inappropriately expressed in the PBs and PGCs of torsoDeg embryos, with frequencies less than those observed in gcl embryos but significantly more than control embryos (27% of torsoDeg embryos express sis-b (n = 16, p=0.043382) and 28% of torsoDeg embryos express Sxl (n = 25, p=0.030307)).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Ectopic upregulation of Sxl and sis-b transcription observed in gcl pole cells is recapitulated in torsoDeg embryos.
source: Thus, ectopic upregulation of Sxl and sis-b transcription observed in gcl pole cells is recapitulated in torsoDeg embryos.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the torsoDeg smFISH experiments.

claim: Ectopic expression of Gcl at the anterior of the embryo downregulates transcription of multiple genes.
source: Taken together with the data reported by Leatherman et al., 2002, our results indicate that ectopic expression of Gcl at the anterior of the embryo downregulates transcription of multiple genes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gcl-bcd-3'UTR experiments and prior studies.

claim: Sxl-Pe is active in scattered nuclei in 43% of torsoDeg male embryos.
source: While female torsoDeg embryos resemble WT, we observed scattered nuclei in which Sxl-Pe is active in 43% of torsoDeg male embryos (Figure 10C, n = 14, p=0.023871).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 10C.

claim: A constitutively active form of the Torso receptor, RL3, turns on Sxl-Pe in males.
source: This finding is also consistent with earlier studies in which we found that a constitutively active form of the Torso receptor, RL3, turns on Sxl-Pe in males (Deshpande, 2004).
evidence: This is a finding from a prior study by the authors, cited in the manuscript.

claim: In the canonical terminal pathway, binding of the Tsl ligand to Torso activates a MAP kinase cascade.
source: In the canonical terminal pathway, binding of the Tsl ligand to Torso activates a MAP kinase cascade that ultimately results in the phosphorylation and subsequent degradation of the transcriptional repressor Capicua by the ERK kinase (de las Heras and Casanova, 2006; Grimm et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the canonical Torso signaling pathway, supported by citations.

claim: The MAP kinase cascade activated by Torso ultimately results in the phosphorylation and subsequent degradation of the transcriptional repressor Capicua by the ERK kinase.
source: In the canonical terminal pathway, binding of the Tsl ligand to Torso activates a MAP kinase cascade that ultimately results in the phosphorylation and subsequent degradation of the transcriptional repressor Capicua by the ERK kinase (de las Heras and Casanova, 2006; Grimm et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the canonical Torso signaling pathway, supported by citations.

claim: Degradation of Capicua results in the transcription of terminal patterning genes, such as tailless.
source: Degradation of Capicua, in turn, results in the transcription of terminal patterning genes, such as tailless.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the canonical Torso signaling pathway.

claim: Maternal deposition of MEKE203K or MEKF53S could not activate Sxl-Pe transcription in pole buds or PGCs.
source: We found that maternal deposition of MEKE203K or MEKF53S could not activate Sxl-Pe transcription in PBs or PGCs (not shown, see Discussion).
evidence: This is a finding from the GOF MEK experiments.

claim: Sxl-Pe expression is activated in male somatic nuclei by the GOF MEK proteins.
source: Nevertheless, we found that, as was observed for torsoDeg, Sxl-Pe expression is activated in male somatic nuclei by the GOF MEK proteins (Figure 10D, 46% of MEKE203K males showed patchy somatic Sxl expression, n = 13, p=0.019079).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 10D.

claim: The canonical Torso signaling pathway is capable of impacting Sxl-Pe promoter activity.
source: Taken together with our previous findings (Deshpande, 2004), this result would argue that the canonical Torso signaling pathway is capable of impacting Sxl-Pe promoter activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the GOF MEK experiments and prior studies.

claim: tailless is not activated in gcl pole buds or PGCs.
source: In this context, it is also interesting to note that a key transcriptional target of the terminal signaling pathway, tailless, is not activated in gcl PBs or PGCs.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claim: tailless is not activated in embryos expressing TorsoDeg or either of the GOF MEK variants.
source: This is also true for embryos expressing TorsoDeg or either of the GOF MEK variants (not shown).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claim: tailless transcription is ectopically activated in pgc mutant PGCs.
source: Since tailless transcription is ectopically activated in pgc mutant PGCs, it would appear that the canonical terminal signaling pathway is not able to overcome the repressive effects of the Pgc protein in the case of tailless, even in a gcl background.
evidence: This is established knowledge about pgc mutant phenotypes.

claim: The canonical terminal signaling pathway is not able to overcome the repressive effects of the Pgc protein in the case of tailless, even in a gcl background.
source: Since tailless transcription is ectopically activated in pgc mutant PGCs, it would appear that the canonical terminal signaling pathway is not able to overcome the repressive effects of the Pgc protein in the case of tailless, even in a gcl background.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that tailless is not activated in gcl or torsoDeg PGCs.

claim: In wild-type embryos, nuclei entering the posterior pole trigger the release of the pole plasm from the posterior cortex of the embryo by a centrosome/microtubule-dependent mechanism.
source: In WT embryos, nuclei entering the posterior pole trigger the release of the pole plasm from the posterior cortex of the embryo by a centrosome/microtubule-dependent mechanism (Lerit and Gavis, 2011; Raff and Glover, 1989).
evidence: This is established knowledge about pole plasm release, supported by citations.

claim: Once released, the pole plasm constituents are distributed within the growing bud by a microtubule-dependent mechanism.
source: Once released, the pole plasm constituents are distributed within the growing bud by a microtubule-dependent mechanism.
evidence: This is established knowledge about pole plasm distribution.

claim: Spreading of pole plasm constituents is restricted to the growing bud in wild-type embryos.
source: However, spreading is restricted to the growing bud and the pole plasm components are ultimately incorporated into newly formed PGCs when the buds cellularize.
evidence: This is established knowledge about pole plasm sequestration.

claim: Pole plasm components are ultimately incorporated into newly formed PGCs when the buds cellularize in wild-type embryos.
source: However, spreading is restricted to the growing bud and the pole plasm components are ultimately incorporated into newly formed PGCs when the buds cellularize.
evidence: This is established knowledge about pole plasm sequestration.

claim: In gcl embryos, nuclear entry triggers the release of the pole plasm from the cortex.
source: In gcl embryos, nuclear entry also triggers the release of the pole plasm from the cortex; however, the pole plasm proteins and mRNAs are not retained in the newly formed PBs after they are released, but instead spread to the cytoplasmic territories of neighboring somatic nuclei along the cortex and also into the interior of the embryo (Lerit et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about gcl mutant phenotypes, supported by citation.

claim: In gcl embryos, pole plasm proteins and mRNAs are not retained in the newly formed pole buds after they are released.
source: In gcl embryos, nuclear entry also triggers the release of the pole plasm from the cortex; however, the pole plasm proteins and mRNAs are not retained in the newly formed PBs after they are released, but instead spread to the cytoplasmic territories of neighboring somatic nuclei along the cortex and also into the interior of the embryo (Lerit et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about gcl mutant phenotypes, supported by citation.

claim: In gcl embryos, pole plasm proteins and mRNAs spread to the cytoplasmic territories of neighboring somatic nuclei along the cortex and into the interior of the embryo.
source: In gcl embryos, nuclear entry also triggers the release of the pole plasm from the cortex; however, the pole plasm proteins and mRNAs are not retained in the newly formed PBs after they are released, but instead spread to the cytoplasmic territories of neighboring somatic nuclei along the cortex and also into the interior of the embryo (Lerit et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about gcl mutant phenotypes, supported by citation.

claim: Vasa and the three pole plasm mRNAs (gcl, pgc, nos) are sequestered in the PGCs of wild-type embryos.
source: As shown in maximum intensity projections and the accompanying distribution graphs, Vasa and the three pole plasm mRNAs are sequestered in the PGCs of WT embryos.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figures 11-14.

claim: In gcl embryos, Vasa protein, and pgc and nos mRNAs spread into the territories occupied by nearby somatic nuclei.
source: In contrast, in gcl embryos, Vasa protein, and pgc and nos mRNAs spread into the territories occupied by nearby somatic nuclei.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figures 11, 13, and 14.

claim: Retention of pole plasm constituents in PGCs is clearly disrupted in gcl embryos.
source: As evident from the profiles of pole plasm distribution for individual embryos, the extent of spreading varies somewhat from embryo to embryo; however, retention of pole plasm constituents in PGCs is clearly disrupted in gcl embryos.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the imaging data.

claim: The effects of torsoDeg on the sequestration of the pole plasm constituents are quite similar to those observed in gcl embryos.
source: Interestingly, as was the case for transcriptional activation, the effects of torsoDeg on the sequestration of the pole plasm constituents are quite similar to those observed in gcl embryos.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the imaging data comparing torsoDeg and gcl embryos.

claim: In early torsoDeg embryos, pole plasm constituents appear to be localized correctly to the posterior pole.
source: In early torsoDeg embryos, pole plasm constituents appear to be localized correctly to the posterior pole (Figure 15).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 15.

claim: After the nuclei migrate to the surface of the embryo, the localization of pole plasm components is disrupted in torsoDeg embryos.
source: However, after the nuclei migrate to the surface of the embryo, the localization of pole plasm components is disrupted.
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging experiments.

claim: Vasa protein and pgc and nos mRNAs spread into the territories of somatic nuclei located along the posterior lateral cortex of torsoDeg embryos.
source: Vasa protein (Figure 11) and pgc (Figure 13) and nos (Figure 14) mRNAs spread into the territories of somatic nuclei located along the posterior lateral cortex of torsoDeg embryos.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figures 11, 13, and 14.

claim: gcl mRNA is not properly restricted in torsoDeg embryos.
source: In addition, gcl mRNA (Figure 12) is not properly restricted in torsoDeg embryos, and like pgc and nos mRNAs, it is distributed along the lateral cortex.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 12.

claim: There exists an antagonistic relationship between torso and gcl.
source: This finding is of special interest as it suggests the existence of an antagonistic relationship between torso and gcl.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that gcl mRNA is mislocalized in torsoDeg embryos.

claim: Torso activity likely controls the sequestration of pole plasm—including gcl mRNA—to the pole buds and PGCs.
source: While gcl negatively regulates the Torso receptor by promoting its degradation, Torso activity likely controls the sequestration of pole plasm—including gcl mRNA—to the PBs and PGCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that pole plasm is mislocalized in torsoDeg embryos.

claim: A mechanism controlling pole plasm sequestration would avoid inappropriate exposure of the neighboring somatic nuclei to gcl RNA (and possibly protein), ultimately ensuring proper germline/soma distinction.
source: Such a mechanism would avoid inappropriate exposure of the neighboring somatic nuclei to gcl RNA (and possibly protein), ultimately ensuring proper germline/soma distinction.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the functional significance of the antagonistic relationship between Torso and Gcl.

claim: MEKE203K or MEKF53S protein induces the inappropriate dispersal of gcl and pgc mRNAs into the surrounding soma in a pattern very similar to that observed in torsoDeg and gcl embryos.
source: As shown in Figure 16, MEKE203K or MEKF53S protein induces the inappropriate dispersal of gcl and pgc mRNAs into the surrounding soma in a pattern very similar to that observed in torsoDeg and gcl embryos.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 16.

claim: The gcl phenotype of pole plasm dispersal appears to depend upon the canonical terminal signal transduction cascade.
source: Thus, this gcl phenotype would appear to depend upon the canonical terminal signal transduction cascade.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the GOF MEK experiments showing pole plasm dispersal.

claim: Shutting off transcription is a critical function of Gcl protein.
source: We show that shutting off transcription is, in fact, a critical function of Gcl protein.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Elimination or reduction in Sxl function ameliorates the gcl defects in PGC formation/specification.
source: In this case, the specification defects in nos embryos can be partially rescued by eliminating Sxl activity (Deshpande et al., 1999). The same is true for gcl mutants: elimination or reduction in Sxl function ameliorates the gcl defects in PGC formation/specification.
evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: The role of Gcl in inhibiting Sxl-Pe transcription is not dependent upon other constituents of the pole plasm.
source: Importantly, the role of Gcl in inhibiting Sxl-Pe transcription is not dependent upon other constituents of the pole plasm.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gcl-bcd-3'UTR experiment.

claim: The rescue of gcl by eliminating the Sxl gene or reducing its activity is not complete.
source: Since the rescue of gcl by eliminating the Sxl gene or reducing its activity is not complete, one would expect that there must be other important gcl targets.
evidence: This is an observation from the Sxl rescue experiments.

claim: There must be other important gcl targets besides Sxl.
source: Since the rescue of gcl by eliminating the Sxl gene or reducing its activity is not complete, one would expect that there must be other important gcl targets.
evidence: This is an inference based on the incomplete rescue of gcl by Sxl removal.

claim: The failure to shut down ongoing transcription in gcl pole buds and PGCs is due (at least in part) to the persistence of the Torso receptor in the absence of Gcl-mediated degradation.
source: Thus, the failure to shut down ongoing transcription in gcl PBs and PGCs must be due (at least in part) to the persistence of the Torso receptor in the absence of Gcl-mediated degradation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the torsoDeg experiments.

claim: The establishment/maintenance of transcriptional silencing in pole buds is a critical function of Gcl.
source: Taken together, these data strongly suggest that the establishment/maintenance of transcriptional silencing in PBs is a critical function of Gcl.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The GOF activity of MEK variants tested is likely not equivalent to the activity from the normal Torso-dependent signaling cascade.
source: However, an important caveat is that the GOF activity of MEK variants we tested is likely not equivalent to the activity from the normal Torso-dependent signaling cascade (Goyal et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a caveat about the interpretation of the GOF MEK experiments, based on citation.

claim: The pole plasm contains at least two other factors that help impose transcriptional quiescence.
source: As the pole plasm contains at least two other factors that help impose transcriptional quiescence, the two GOF MEK mutants we tested may simply not be sufficient to overcome their repressive functions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about pole plasm components (nos and pgc).

claim: The two GOF MEK mutants tested may not be sufficient to overcome the repressive functions of other pole plasm factors.
source: As the pole plasm contains at least two other factors that help impose transcriptional quiescence, the two GOF MEK mutants we tested may simply not be sufficient to overcome their repressive functions.
evidence: This is a speculation about why GOF MEK did not activate transcription in PGCs.

claim: A viable GOF mutation in Torso can induce ectopic activation of Sxl-Pe in male somatic nuclei, but is unable to activate Sxl-Pe in PGCs.
source: The same is true for a viable GOF mutation in Torso: it can induce ectopic activation of Sxl-Pe in male somatic nuclei, but is unable to activate Sxl-Pe in PGCs (Deshpande, 2004).
evidence: This is a finding from a prior study by the authors, cited in the manuscript.

claim: There are reasons to think that the canonical Torso signal transduction cascade must be inhibited for proper PGC formation.
source: There are also reasons to think that the canonical Torso signal transduction cascade must be inhibited for proper PGC formation.
evidence: This is a statement about the interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The Tsl→Torso→ERK pathway may have other non-transcriptional targets that can interfere with pole bud/PGC formation.
source: However, this result does not exclude the possibility that the Tsl→Torso→ERK pathway has other non-transcriptional targets that, like Sxl-Pe expression, can also interfere with PB/PGC formation.
evidence: This is a speculation about alternative mechanisms.

claim: A potential target of the Torso signaling pathway is the microtubule cytoskeleton.
source: In this respect, a potential—if not likely—target is the microtubule cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is a speculation based on prior findings about gcl mutants.

claim: The pole bud and PGC formation defects as well as the failure to properly sequester critical germline determinants in gcl arise from abnormalities in microtubule/centrosome organization.
source: In previous studies, we found that the PB and PGC formation defects as well as the failure to properly sequester critical germline determinants in gcl arise from abnormalities in microtubule/centrosome organization (Lerit et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from a prior study by the authors, cited in the manuscript.

claim: Preliminary imaging experiments indicate that centrosome distribution of torsoDeg pole buds is abnormal.
source: Preliminary imaging experiments indicate that centrosome distribution of torsoDeg PBs is also abnormal, suggesting that inappropriate activation of the terminal signaling pathway perturbs the organization or functioning of the microtubule cytoskeleton and/or centrosomes.
evidence: This is a preliminary finding from the study.

claim: Inappropriate activation of the terminal signaling pathway perturbs the organization or functioning of the microtubule cytoskeleton and/or centrosomes.
source: Preliminary imaging experiments indicate that centrosome distribution of torsoDeg PBs is also abnormal, suggesting that inappropriate activation of the terminal signaling pathway perturbs the organization or functioning of the microtubule cytoskeleton and/or centrosomes.
evidence: This is an inference based on preliminary imaging data.

claim: A receptor-dependent MEK/ERK signaling cascade promotes centrosome accumulation of γ-tubulin and microtubule nucleation in mammalian tissue culture cells.
source: While further experiments will be required to demonstrate microtubule and centrosomal aberrations in torsoDeg and GOF MEK embryos, a role for a receptor-dependent MEK/ERK signaling cascade in promoting centrosome accumulation of γ-tubulin and microtubule nucleation has been documented in mammalian tissue culture cells (Colello et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge from mammalian cell biology, supported by citation.

claim: MEK/ERK signaling may have a similar role in Drosophila pole bud nuclei and PGCs as it does in mammalian tissue culture cells.
source: It is thus conceivable that MEK/ERK signaling has a similar role in Drosophila PB nuclei and PGCs.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the mammalian cell biology findings.

claim: The data reveal a mutual antagonism between the determinants that specify germline versus somatic identity.
source: Taken together, our data reveal a mutual antagonism between the determinants that specify germline versus somatic identity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.
